The map's label for the Muslim sultanates of the Malay peninsula and the islands of Indonesia, shown from 1492 to 1600. Islam spread along the trade routes, carried by merchants and teachers, and port rulers who converted gained trading partners across the Indian Ocean. Malay became the common language of trade.

The leader was the Malacca Sultanate until Portugal took Malacca in 1511. Its place was then shared by rivals:

  • Johor, founded by the heirs of Malacca's royal house;
  • Aceh in north Sumatra, enemy of the Portuguese;
  • Brunei on Borneo, at its height in the early 1500s;
  • Demak and Banten on Java;
  • Ternate and Tidore in the clove islands of Maluku. Ternate threw out the Portuguese in 1575.

From 1565 Spain, newly in the Philippines, fought the Muslim sultanates of the south.
